title: Ponticianus and Anthony (8.6)
hook: hearing of Anthony, Augustine is ashamed that the unlearned rise up
tomorrow: can you want something and not want it at the same time?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Victorinus, and his name whispered through a church in Rome. Your line: in public.

The person who sees most clearly what to do isn't always the one with the degrees. Sometimes it's the custodian, the grandmother, the kid who just does the kind thing. Augustine learns that at home in Milan. A visitor named Ponticianus, a fellow African with a post at the emperor's court, spots a book on the game table, opens it, and finds the letters of Paul. He smiles. Then he starts talking about a monk from the deserts of Egypt named Anthony, and two professors find out what a monk can teach them.
screen: `NOT ALWAYS THE ONE WITH DEGREES.` → `PAUL ON THE GAME TABLE.` → `A MONK FROM EGYPT.`

segments.voice: First, Anthony. Ponticianus is amazed that Augustine and his friend Alypius have never heard of him. They also hadn't known about a monastery just outside the walls of Milan, under Ambrose's care. Second, an afternoon at Trier. Ponticianus once went walking there with friends. Two of them wandered into a small house where some servants of God lived, and found a book: the life of Anthony. One began to read, and before he finished he decided to leave his career at court and serve God. His friend joined him on the spot. Third, Augustine's face. While Ponticianus talks, Augustine says, God was turning him around to look at himself, at the life he had kept behind his own back so he wouldn't have to see it. Fourth, the cry. When the visitor leaves, he turns on Alypius. In his Latin: surgunt indocti et caelum rapiunt. The unlearned rise up and take heaven by force, and here we are, with all our learning. The shame isn't the end of him. It's the beginning of the turn.
screen: `THEY'D NEVER HEARD OF ANTHONY.` · `AN AFTERNOON AT TRIER.` · `TURNED TO SEE HIMSELF.` · `THE UNLEARNED RISE UP.` · then, large: `THE UNLEARNED RISE.`

segments.voice: Write by hand the name of someone who lives goodness more simply than you could explain it, and under the name, one thing they actually do. Then spend the sit just looking at those two lines. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.
Ponticianus and Anthony. A visitor's stories about a desert monk, and a professor ashamed that the unlearned rise first.
The unlearned rise, and sometimes the simplest life is the clearest teacher in the room. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1447 COUNTS.` → `THE CONFESSIONS, READ THROUGH · 21 OF 35.` → `TOMORROW: CAN YOU WANT SOMETHING AND NOT WANT IT AT THE SAME TIME?`

howItsDone: Catholics read the lives of the saints, Anthony of Egypt among them, as examples to learn from, and the Church teaches that every baptized person, learned or not, is called to holiness.

fork.setup: you're tutoring a younger kid in math, and you find out she visits her sick neighbor every day after school. what would Augustine's reaction to Anthony suggest?
options: let her goodness teach you something your learning hasn't.
keep it to math; how she lives isn't your subject.
teach her that real goodness needs good arguments.
fork.reveal: Augustine, the professor, was shaken by people who simply did the thing. The unlearned rise up, he cried, and here we are with all our learning.

original.note: Latin, Confessions 8.8: the unlearned rise up and take heaven by force.

trapdoor: what you thought: Augustine was converted by clever arguments.
what it means: he was shaken by stories of people who simply acted, while he kept thinking.

what a scholar hears: the Life of Anthony at work inside the Confessions; 'surgunt indocti et caelum rapiunt' (8.8), which some readers hear as an echo of the kingdom of heaven taken by force in Matthew 11:12.

chat.says: dad said 'we'll talk.' so i asked abuela first. she said 'Dios te cuida allá también.' why's that enough?
options: The unlearned rise, Augustine said. Abuela isn't explaining; she's living it, and that can be clearer than a list.
It isn't, really. Augustine says wisdom comes from study, so keep making your pros and cons list.
She's being vague. Augustine was ashamed of simple people, so trust your own analysis over hers.
chat.meaning: Hearing of Anthony, Augustine the professor cried: the unlearned rise up. A life lived simply can be clearer than any argument.

Ponticianus.meaning: an African Christian at the emperor's court who visited Augustine

Anthony.meaning: a monk of Egypt whose life story inspired many

Trier.meaning: a Roman imperial city, now in Germany
